title: Toward global food security: Transforming OCP through analytics
contribution: An Edelman-style account of a multiperiod MIO, built with Dynamic Ideas (cofounded by Bertsimas), that plans OCP's whole chain from mines to port. It runs in under a minute for monthly planning. By the model's own counterfactuals against the company's pre-2006 siloed rules, it added over $2.3 billion of EBITDA in 2015–2020.
problem_entry: {AP + IO; LO and CP as engines} Before 2006 OCP's departments planned in silos (sales by highest unit margin, mining by volume), and the company was in financial distress (pp. 4, 6). Problem: one multiperiod MIO from mines to port that maximizes the margin on variable cost, with secondary objectives (pp. 6–7).
key_idea: All major operational decisions on one decision platform with one corporate objective (p. 3). The modelling answers several objectives, substitute products and nonlinear joint-venture dynamics (p. 6), and uses general variables for any number of products and for what-if changes to the network (p. 15).
assumptions: Deterministic contracts with minimum and maximum volumes and a price, with product substitution (pp. 7, 15); a product at the port meets demand at once (p. 7). The data had to be standardized from scratch in 2011 (pp. 7–8).
proof_devices: semicontinuous production via binaries (minVol·δ ≤ extract ≤ δ·maxVol) and a cap on the number of products per facility (p. 16)
switch indicators linked by 1 + δswitch ≥ βprod(t) + βprod(t − 1), whose wasted capacity is charged inside the capacity constraint (p. 17)
second-order cone storage dynamics, omitted from the appendix, and binary stack variables for storage halls (pp. 15, 17)
daily model: tighter-relaxation formulations, heuristic starts from boat pre-assignment or coarser time grids, and Gurobi callbacks that shift effort between feasibility and optimality (p. 8)
experiments: Monthly model: about 6,500 rows and 6,000 columns (440 integer), 0.5 s of optimization and 31 s per single-period run. The daily model (600,000 rows, 60,000 binaries) has larger gaps that are not quantified (p. 8). Impact comes from in-model counterfactuals: for 2020, $200M + $130M + $60M + $60M + $40M = $490M (pp. 10–11). 2015 rests on a confidential consulting report and 2016 is imputed; the total is $2,330M of $9,855M EBITDA (Table 1, p. 11). The introduction says 23.2% (p. 4), elsewhere 23.6%; Table 1's 24.0% for 2020 should be 24.3% [my computation].
positioning: Cites mine-planning and supply-chain OR (Graves et al., Newman et al., Bodon et al.) but holds that OCP's problem needed a novel modelling approach (p. 6). Off-the-shelf corporate planning tools were found lacking (p. 9).
writing: Impact first: dollars and EBITDA shares in the abstract, then sections on culture, food security, education and portability. The body describes the model without mathematics; the formulation is in an appendix (pp. 2, 6, 15).
limits_future: Extensions under test: extraction and boat scheduling, a daily model, a robust and adaptive version of the same size, a CAPEX model (pp. 8–9). Limits are not discussed [my reading]: the counterfactuals come from the authors' own model, 2015 and 2016 are not computed, and the authors are the consultant and the client.

method_links.note: The baseline is the owner's pre-2006 rule (higher-margin-first sales, siloed operations), and the score is EBITDA. The model has been the primary platform since 2015 and is run by OCP teams. The counterfactual is the model's own re-run, not an observed outcome.

Adoption is carried by Dynamic Ideas, a company he cofounded. The case is taught in an MIT Sloan executive class that he teaches with OCP's CEO, and portability to a steel maker and an airline is claimed.
The MIO with second-order cone constraints stays in class, with solve times printed. The robust and adaptive extension is said to scale to the same sizes as the deterministic model.
Heuristic starts and tighter formulations are used for the daily model, but its gaps are only called larger and never quantified.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The deployment's 2020 value is split into five capabilities, each compared in turn with the owner's old rule and then summed ($490M). The authors flag the comparison that overestimates.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: staged deployment from a spreadsheet proof of concept
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A 2008 Excel single-period LP with one mine, one treatment plant and one chemical facility; MIO components from 2011; the full version deployed in 2015; further modules under test.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimization model as an organizational alignment device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Quarterly committees of sales, mining and chemical staff plan on the model; joint decisions rest on its calculations rather than on qualitative discussion.

transferable: Attribute a deployed model's value to separable capabilities. Switch one capability off at a time against the owner's old rule, sum the parts, and say which comparison flatters the model (pp. 10–11).

When a large daily MIO stalls at the root relaxation, build starting solutions from a coarser time grid or a pre-assignment, and use callbacks to move the solver between feasibility and optimality (p. 8).
Begin with a spreadsheet LP covering one mine, one plant and one chemical facility. Grow the MIO module by module and deploy it progressively: components from 2011, the full version in 2015 (p. 8).
coauthors: Adrian Becker, Kassem Benabderrazik, Nada Chtinna, Nada El Majdoub, El Miloudi Mahboubi, Driss Lahlou Kitane, Steve Kokkotos, Georgia Mourtzinou, Ilyas Rakhis

quotes.text: We had to experiment with different formulations to identify those that yield tighter relaxations and with heuristics to create appropriate starting solutions so that Gurobi would avoid long delays at the root relaxation.

we compared the revenue generated through the multiperiod comprehensive planning of the current model with the revenue that would have been generated under the siloed approach that the company followed before the transformation.

title: Data-driven interpretable policy construction for personalized mobile health
contribution: A batch off-policy pipeline for HeartSteps anti-sedentary messages. It has three parts: doubly robust counterfactuals; a learned threshold rule; and OPT+, an Optimal Policy Tree trained with a per-message budget penalty and gated by the threshold rule. On test users it cuts estimated daily sedentary time from 148.02 to about 104–109 minutes, with about half the messages, and its tree is interpretable and stable.
problem_entry: {DA + ML + AP} HeartSteps samples eligible sedentary times uniformly (target 1.5 messages a day) and does not try to maximize the treatment effect (abstract; p. 1). Goal: fewer sedentary minutes with fewer messages, through a policy that behavioural scientists can read (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Three steps: doubly robust outcomes (pp. 4–5); a per-message threshold on the estimated effect, personal or pooled (pp. 5–6); OPT+, which sends a message only when an OPT tree trained on λ-penalized outcomes and the threshold rule agree and sending is feasible (p. 6). Parameters are chosen on user-daily validation metrics (pp. 6–7).
assumptions: A contextual bandit per user. A message's effect lasts at most two hours, and a daily budget N ∈ {1, 2} handles disengagement (pp. 1, 3, 5). Data: 51 of 94 users, up to 80 days each, 103 features; the outcome is minutes until non-sedentary, capped at 120 (pp. 3–4). The feasibility indicator prints r_it where 1 − r_it seems meant [my reading] (pp. 3–4).
proof_devices: evaluation ground truth from XGBoost outcome models trained on the test set only, applied to every policy including the logged current policy (p. 5)
doubly robust outcomes with the trial's known randomization probabilities, trimmed to [0, 120] (p. 5)
points with no message now but a message within two hours excluded from outcome training (p. 5)
budget entered as a per-message penalty λ (or λ_i = αΓ_i) in tree training, with the hard constraint only at execution (p. 6)
experiments: Per average user and day: the current policy gives 148.02 sedentary minutes with 1.62 messages; the fixed threshold with budget 1 gives 103.98 with 0.79; OPT+ with a fixed λ gives 108.56 with 0.76. Personalization brings no benefit (p. 7). The top 7 of the tree's 15 variables recur in at least half of 100 retrained trees (Table II, p. 8). Julia on a MacBook Pro; no run times (p. 7).
positioning: Contrasts with online bandit apps, and with batch policy learning that fixes a policy class (Athey–Wager) or uses black-box forests (Sun–Du–Wager). Builds on Optimal Policy Trees for global optimality and scalability (pp. 2–3).
writing: A three-item contribution list (p. 2). A recommendations section addresses behavioural scientists with hypotheses to test, such as heart rate as a sign of stress (pp. 8–9). The word significant is used for means whose 95% intervals separate (p. 7).
limits_future: Stated: 51 of 94 participants (possible bias), a deterministic binary policy, a batch proof of concept. Proposes an online version with warm-started retraining (p. 9). Not stated [my reading]: every number, including the current policy's, is a model estimate, and nothing was field-tested.

method_links.note: The owner's current algorithm is the baseline, and the scores are decision metrics (sedentary minutes, messages). The policy is built for the trial's scientists to read, and the paper calls itself a proof of concept to be tested online.

The message budget (N, λ, α) is the knob, and Fig. 1 plots sedentary time against messages. But only six discrete variants are shown, and OPT+ is called comparable to the threshold rule though 4.6 minutes worse [my computation]. A negative result is printed in the body: personalization brings no benefit (Heuristic 4).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A message is sent only when the interpretable tree and the personalized threshold rule agree. S370 in this batch prescribes only on a majority vote of seven models.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: evaluation oracle fitted on the test fold only
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Outcome models trained only on test data score every policy, including the incumbent's logged actions.
100 trees trained with perturbed parameters; the recurrence of each split variable is reported. S365 in this batch measures stability over 100 bootstrap fits.

transferable: Score every policy, including the incumbent's logged actions, with outcome models fitted only on the test fold. The evaluator then shares nothing with the learner (p. 5).
Enter a resource budget into tree training as a per-action penalty λ, or a user-scaled λ_i = αΓ_i, and enforce the hard budget only at execution (p. 6).
Act only when an interpretable tree and a personalized threshold rule agree. The policy becomes more conservative and stays readable (p. 6).
Audit an interpretable policy's stability: retrain about 100 trees with perturbed parameters and report how often each split variable recurs (Table II, p. 8).
coauthors: Predrag Klasnja, Susan Murphy, Liangyuan Na

quotes.text: HeartSteps uses an algorithm to uniformly spread out the daily message budget over time, but does not attempt to maximize treatment effects.
We observe that personalization does not bring a benefit over fixed thresholds.

title: Improving quality in cardiothoracic surgery: exploiting the untapped potential of machine learning
contribution: An editorial written with STS leaders. It proposes NLP-based automated extraction of registry fields from EHRs, so that the STS database can grow in variables without more manual burden and can feed nonlinear, multimodal and interpretable risk models.
problem_entry: {AP + ML; DA as the aim} The STS registry is near-universal and accurate. Richer ML risk models need more variables, but participants refuse more manual collection, and STS has already cut the required fields (pp. 1, 3).
key_idea: NLP extraction from structured and unstructured EHR data into STS fields, with data managers reviewing each hospital file, so that variables can be added at little or no extra cost (pp. 3–5; Figure 1, p. 4).
assumptions: No model. The data are the STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database (nearly 8 million records) and hospital EHRs, which differ across organizations, have missing or inaccurate elements and keep much in free text (pp. 2–3).
experiments: None. The editorial cites that ML has improved cardiothoracic risk prediction only marginally so far (p. 3), and that early ensemble and tree-based studies improved risk estimation (p. 4).
positioning: Presents the STS database as a gold-standard registry. Earlier neural-network risk models (Lippmann and Shahian 1997) were only modestly successful. The group's own mitral-valve, coronary-artery and POTTER papers are cited as early evidence (pp. 2, 4, 6).
writing: An editorial that opens with an aphorism variously attributed to Einstein and Ford (p. 1). It has headed sections, a vision figure, a section on perils and a closing call for collaboration (pp. 1–5).
limits_future: Perils named: few studies show gains in accuracy, practice or cost; opacity; EHR errors propagating into the models; bias; the need for external validation across several centres (p. 5).

method_links.note: The programme is carried by a professional society, its registry and four academic centres, with STS funding, rather than by a course or a company. It hopes to set a paradigm for other national registries.

The owner (STS) and its current rule (manual curation of a reduced variable set) are named, but the targets are prediction metrics (discrimination, calibration), not decisions. The central proposal is Heuristic 6: build the data asset.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: automate data collection to break the trade-off between burden and dimension
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: NLP extraction of registry fields with a human review of each file, so that the registry can add variables at near-zero marginal cost.

transferable: When the cost of collecting data blocks richer models, automate the extraction and keep a human review of each file, so that variables can be added at near-zero marginal cost (pp. 3, 5).
In the piece that launches a programme, list its perils too: error propagation from the source data, bias, and external validation across centres (p. 5).
coauthors: Agni Orfanoudaki, Joseph A. Dearani, David M. Shahian, Vinay Badhwar, Felix Fernandez, Robert Habib, Michael E. Bowdish

quotes.text: Is there a way to minimize the data collection burden while at the same time collecting even more extensive data?

Despite numerous publications that highlight the potential opportunities and benefits derived from the deployment of ML in cardiac surgery, few studies have demonstrated substantial improvements in risk model predictive accuracy, clinical practice, or cost.

title: Stable classification
contribution: Extends stable regression to classification: train against the worst-case training subset of size k. Three solvers: an LP-dual robust counterpart (SVM becomes an LP, LR stays convex), cutting planes, and a one-shot Monte Carlo scenario sample, which also covers RF and OCT. Across 30 UCI data sets it reports better output stability and, for SVM, higher average accuracy at comparable run times.
problem_entry: {ML + RO; LO and CP as engines} Models change with the training/validation split and with new data (pp. 1–2). Breiman asked for a more stable single-tree CART; RF and SVM were assumed stable (pp. 2–4).
key_idea: Minimize over models the maximum, over all k-subsets, of the summed loss (p. 8). It is solved three ways: a robust counterpart (SVM, LR), cutting planes, and Monte Carlo over ζ sampled subsets (pp. 9–12). Stability is measured as output, structural and hyperparameter spread over 100 bootstrap fits (pp. 6–7).
assumptions: Hinge, logistic and 1 − p(true label) losses (Table 2, p. 8). The worst case is chosen over an average case for computational efficiency (p. 9). The k used in the experiments, and how RF and OCT are trained on the min–max, are not stated [my reading]. 30 UCI data sets (p. 12).
proof_devices: the inner maximum over {Σz = k, z binary} equals the maximum over its convex hull; LP duality gives min kθ + Σu_i s.t. θ + u_i ≥ f_i, u ≥ 0 (Problems 4–5, pp. 9–10)
the stable SVM is an LP and the stable LR a convex program (Problems 6–7, p. 10)
cutting-plane epigraph method that adds the most violated subset, with convergence credited to Fletcher–Leyffer (p. 11)
Monte Carlo sampling of ζ subsets, with probabilistic feasibility credited to Calafiore–Campi (p. 12)
[my reading] the objective equals the sum of the k largest training losses (pp. 9–10)
experiments: 30 UCI sets, a 90/10 split, 100 bootstraps, ζ = 20 (pp. 12–13). Averages: SVM accuracy 0.773 → 0.807 (robust counterpart); LR stability improves while accuracy goes 0.672 → 0.668; RF changes are small, and its structural stability worsens under cutting planes (0.004 → 0.012); for OCT the original is best on accuracy and hyperparameter stability (Tables 3–10, pp. 14–17). Relative run times: robust counterpart 0.31–0.49, cutting planes up to 8.9 (Table 11, p. 17). [my computation] The robust counterpart beats the original SVM on 6 data sets, loses on 7 and ties on 17, and five data sets where the original scored 0.500–0.629 carry the gain (Table 12, p. 22). Table 16's caption repeats the SVM averages (p. 26). No significance tests and no CART or DRO baseline.
positioning: Extends Bertsimas–Paskov stable regression. Contrasts with bagging, boosting and RF (stable by averaging but uninterpretable), with Last et al. (stable but inaccurate), and with DRO methods, which it calls less flexible and less efficient without testing them (pp. 2–4).
writing: The abstract's two claims, (a) and (b), recur nearly verbatim in the introduction and conclusion (pp. 1–2, 18). The word surprisingly marks the RF result (pp. 1, 4). A conjecture explains the faster run times (p. 17), and the conclusion urges practitioners to adopt the method (p. 19).
limits_future: Claims gains in stability, and sometimes in accuracy, at comparable run times, and suggests that current training sits at an interior point of the performance/stability Pareto curve (p. 19). Limits and future work are not discussed [my reading].

method_links.note: The worst-case set is chosen because it keeps the class: the stable SVM is an LP and the stable LR stays convex. The paper prints that the counterpart exists only for these two.
Stability is the property and k the knob, but k is never varied and no price curve is drawn. The trade-off claim rests on averages over 30 data sets.

The duel is only against each method's nominal version [my reading]: no CART (Breiman's question) and no DRO baseline (the efficiency claim). OCT is listed as solved to optimality without a reported certificate (Tension T1).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Output, structural and hyperparameter stability over 100 bootstrap fits on one test set. S353 in this batch reports variable recurrence over 100 retrained trees.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: the data split as the uncertain parameter
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The training subset is the uncertainty, with the training-set size k as its budget, so that robust optimization replaces averaging over random splits.

transferable: To be robust to the training split, minimize the worst case over all k-subsets. The dual of the inner LP gives kθ + Σu_i with θ + u_i ≥ loss_i, which keeps a linear or convex loss in its class (pp. 9–10).
Where no counterpart exists (trees, forests), solve once over ζ ≈ 20 sampled subsets, and plot the metrics against ζ to show that they settle (pp. 12–13, 18).

Report stability three ways over 100 bootstrap fits on one fixed test set: variance of predicted probabilities, spread of coefficients or variable importances, and spread of tuned hyperparameters (pp. 6–7).

quotes.text: Our choice to minimize over the worst-case training error rather than an average-case is primarily motivated by computational efficiency
perhaps the current approaches to training algorithms have been operating at an interior point with respect to the performance/stability Pareto curve.

title: Ensemble machine learning for personalized antihypertensive treatment
contribution: A prescription rule for antihypertensive regimens from Boston Medical Center EHRs. It combines cardinality matching across six regimens, per-regimen outcome models from seven ML families, and a majority vote that defers to the physician when no majority forms. For patients whose recommendation differs from their actual treatment, the authors' models estimate a 15% lower next blood-pressure score. Read from the August 2020 author manuscript.
problem_entry: {DA + ML + AP} Guidelines recommend first-line drug classes for the whole population, and practice is trial and error (pp. 2–3). EHR-based individualized rules for hypertension are relatively unexplored; the obstacles are counterfactuals, confounding and multiple treatments (p. 4).
key_idea: Regress and compare: seven models per regimen (LASSO, SVR, CART, RF, GBM, ORT, OPT). A majority vote decides, the agreeing models' predictions are averaged, and below a majority the case is deferred (pp. 12–13). Generalized propensity scores check common support, and cardinality matching, an integer program, matches every arm to the smallest one (pp. 11–12).
assumptions: BMC EHR (150,776 patients, 1982–2017); final cohort 19,926 observations in six regimens, 90 variables (pp. 5–6, 9–10). The outcome is a frequency-weighted AHA class score (p. 6). Strong ignorability on observed covariates (pp. 11, 21). Eq. 2 prints Y1 in both terms [my reading] (p. 10).
proof_devices: generalized propensity scores by multinomial logistic regression to confirm common support (p. 11)
cardinality matching via designmatch, matched to the smallest arm: 75% of the data kept, 33 of 34 covariates below 0.25 standardized difference (pp. 11–12, 14)
prescription R² on concordant cases, and PE/PR with each model in turn as an alternate ground truth, both adopted from [24] (pp. 14–16)
experiments: Per-regimen R² 0.15–0.50 unmatched and 0.22–0.49 matched, with OPT weakest (Tables 6–7, pp. 14–15). Prescription R² is 0.60 and 0.55 on concordant cases, roughly 6–8% of the test set [my computation from p. 17]. PE is 15.02% overall, from 4.39% (LASSO) to 21.41% (OPT) (Table 8, p. 16). Subgroup R² is 0.74 for Caucasian and 0.38 for Black patients (Table 12, p. 19).
positioning: Places itself in the potential-outcomes framework and regress-and-compare, citing kNN, causal trees and forests, and optimal prescriptive trees. It follows [24], the coronary-artery framework, and departs from it by deferring to the physician (pp. 3–5).
writing: Four bulleted contributions (pp. 4–5); a worked example of the vote with a seven-by-six table of predictions (p. 13); a first-of-its-kind claim in the conclusion (p. 21); a limitations section (pp. 20–21).
limits_future: Stated: one centre; no diet, activity or adherence data; matching handles only observed confounders (pp. 20–21). The framework could expand as data grow (p. 21). Not stated [my reading]: the improvement is predicted by the same models that choose the treatment, and the gap between Black and Caucasian patients is not framed as a fairness question.

method_links.note: The baseline is the physician's actual prescription (the current allocation), and the score is a decision metric, the next blood-pressure score. The evaluation runs on model predictions, and the paper calls its R² device limited.
No exact model or certificate; seven models vote instead. The group's own OPT is printed as the weakest predictor and the most optimistic prescriber, a negative result in the body (Heuristic 4).
The design of the observational study is itself an integer program (cardinality matching); the device is borrowed (refs. 41, 43).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A treatment is recommended only when at least four of seven models agree; otherwise the physician decides. S353 in this batch also gates its actions on agreement.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: alternate ground truths for a benefit estimate
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Each model is taken in turn as the truth (PE/PR), showing the range of estimated benefit from 4.39% to 21.41%.

transferable: For an observational comparison of several treatments, match every arm to the smallest arm by cardinality matching (maximum matched size subject to pairwise balance), and check standardized mean differences below 0.25 (pp. 11–12, 14).
Prescribe only on a majority across model families, and average the agreeing predictions. Below a majority, return the case to the clinician (p. 13).

Report the estimated benefit with each model taken in turn as the ground truth (PE/PR), so that the reader sees the range from the most conservative model to the most optimistic one (Table 8, pp. 15–16).
coauthors: Alison Borenstein, Antonin Dauvin, Agni Orfanoudaki

quotes.text: The final R2 metric is based on instances for which the treatment suggested by the algorithm matches the patient’s actual treatment, thereby allowing us to know the ground truth outcome for comparison.

For patients for whom the algorithm recommendation differs from the standard of care, we demonstrate an approximate 15% decrease in next blood pressure based on the predicted outcome under the recommended treatment.

title: Machine learning reimagined: the promise of interpretability to combat bias
contribution: A surgical perspective. An Optimal Classification Tree for post-acute care after trauma exposed race at proximal nodes, and the authors argue that interpretable ML can diagnose and mitigate the biases that black boxes would encode.
problem_entry: {ML + AP; fairness} Accurate models can encode bias (p. 1). The authors' OCT for post-acute care placed race at several proximal nodes, with a predicted need of 60.79% against 35% at one node (p. 1; the caption gives 60.70%, p. 2).
key_idea: Interpretability lets users see sensitive variables and act on them. Two remedies are named: drop the attribute (proxies remain) or fairness-adjust the data (pp. 1–2).
assumptions: No model is described: no data set, cohort size or accuracy is given. Bias is said to enter through unrepresentative training data or through data from unequal systems (p. 1).
experiments: None. Whether a fairness-adjusted model was built is not reported [my reading].
positioning: Cites recidivism prediction, Obermeyer et al.'s population-health algorithm and dermatology AI as cases of encoded bias. POTTER is the only methods reference (pp. 1–2).
writing: A first-person cautionary tale in the surgeons' voice, with one figure and a one-paragraph summary (pp. 1–2).
limits_future: Recommends interpretable ML to diagnose and mitigate disparities (p. 2), and grants that interpretability is not essential for imaging (p. 1). It claims parity of OCT with black boxes, with no citation in that sentence [my reading] (p. 1).

method_links.note: Fairness and interpretability are the properties named, but there is no knob and no price: the accuracy cost of fairness adjustment is not reported.

The decision (post-acute care placement) and the clinicians who act on it are named, and interpretability is asked for where people act (Taste mark 5). There is no evaluation against current practice.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: interpretable model as a bias audit
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The fitted tree is read for sensitive variables at proximal nodes, and for the risk gaps they create, before any use.

transferable: Before deploying a clinical model, inspect the fitted interpretable tree for sensitive attributes near the root, and for the gaps in predicted risk they create at each node (p. 1; Figure 1, p. 2).
Where removing a sensitive attribute leaves proxies, fairness-adjust the training data so that decisions agree across groups (p. 2).
coauthors: Lydia R. Maurer, Haytham M. A. Kaafarani

quotes.text: The interpretable OCT methodology enabled us to uncover this bias in our data and algorithms.

For AI problems like imaging or video analysis, model interpretability is not essential, as the process by which pixels are analyzed and generated into an output is not inherently amenable to interpretation.

title: Sparse regression over clusters: SparClur
contribution: SparClur fits sparse ridge regressions in the leaves of an optimal regression tree under one common support. It is an MIO over a shared binary support vector, solved by outer approximation with warm starts from a relaxation. It recovers true supports at n = 100,000 and p = 50,000 in seconds. On medical data it uses about 9 shared features per leaf, with R² within 0.016 of leaf-wise Lasso. Read from the December 2020 manuscript.
problem_entry: {ML + IO; AP} ORT leaf models are fitted by Lasso, which picks many false features, and separately fitted leaves may use a variable in some leaves only, which the paper calls medically implausible (pp. 2–3). Problem (1.1): ridge least squares per cluster with ||w_j||_0 ≤ q and one common support (p. 2).
key_idea: One binary support vector s for all leaves. The problem is convex in s (Lemma 1) and is solved by outer approximation with closed-form dual cuts and lazy callbacks, warm-started by a min–max convex relaxation (pp. 4–6). J = 1 recovers Bertsimas–Van Parys (p. 3).
assumptions: Synthetic Gaussian data (n = 60–800, p = 2,000, J up to 20, SNR 20), plus a variant with partly different supports (pp. 6–9). Real data: BMC glucose, two Framingham tasks and King County prices (p. 11). The partition comes from a point-prediction ORT (p. 12). γ is said to be chosen by the highest MSE on held-out data; the lowest seems meant [my reading] (p. 7).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: the problem equals a minimization over binary s with 1ᵀs ≤ q of a sum over clusters of terms y_jᵀ(I + γ Σ_i s_i K_ij)^{-1} y_j, proved by the argument of [4, Lemma 1] (p. 4)
closed-form duals α_j = (I + γK_j)^{-1} y_j give subgradient cuts; a capacitance matrix avoids the n × n inverse (p. 5)
outer approximation (Duran–Grossmann) with lazy callbacks (pp. 5–6)
convex relaxation by a min–max swap, whose inner problem is solved by the top-q indices, used as a warm start (p. 5)
experiments: CPLEX 12.10 on a Ryzen 9 3950X (p. 6). With five leaves the phase transition comes at about 300 observations, against 600 for separate leaves (p. 7). n = 100,000 and p = 50,000 take 1.7–19.9 s with full recovery (Table 3.1, p. 9). Real data run under a two-minute limit (p. 12): Lasso has the strictly highest R² in 21 of 24 depth rows (one tie), and exact SparClur is within 0.016 [my computation, Tables 4.1–4.4, pp. 12–13]. A glucose leaf uses 8.8 shared features against 21.2 for Lasso (Table 4.5, p. 14). The uncoordinated rival is solved by its relaxation only (p. 12).
positioning: Builds on Bertsimas–Van Parys exact sparse regression and on ORT. Criticizes Lasso's false positives, citing best subset selection, and says no approach had combined IO regression with trees (p. 3).
writing: Three key questions for the synthetic study (p. 6), answered by a numbered list of findings (pp. 9–10). The abstract claims recovery in seconds and a substantial gain in interpretability at a low cost to accuracy (p. 1).
limits_future: Claims correctness, scalability, and gains when observations are few (p. 15). Prints the bad case of differing supports (pp. 9–10) and no lift from depth for stroke (p. 15). Code is released; the medical data cannot be shared (pp. 4, 15). No future work is given.

method_links.note: A medical requirement for interpretability (the same variables in every leaf) becomes one binary support vector in an MIO that is convex in s. It is solved by outer approximation, reusing the J = 1 device of [4].

Interpretability is priced. The knob is q (at most 10, a number clinicians can read, tuned by cross-validation). The price is the R² gap to Lasso and to separately fitted sparse leaves, and the bad case of differing supports is printed.

The exact solve is warm-started by the relaxation and runs under a stated time limit, but no gap is reported, and the uncoordinated rival gets the relaxation instead of the exact solver, so the budgets differ.
Repeats [4]'s point that phase transitions put in question the belief that exact algorithms cannot match heuristics at scale. No speed-up figure is rebuilt.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The leaf models of one tree must use the same variables, imposed through one binary support vector, as a structural interpretability device.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: phase transition as a sample-size design rule

transferable: When the models of several segments must use the same variables, impose one binary support vector across all segments. In the kernel form the objective stays convex in s, so outer approximation applies (pp. 2–5).
Get warm starts from the min–max convex relaxation, whose inner maximization is solved by picking the q largest scores (p. 5).
Report interpretability beside accuracy: features per leaf (minimum, maximum, mean), and how many features recur in more than half of the leaves (Table 4.5, p. 14).
Use the phase transition as a design rule: compute how many observations each segment needs before the exact method becomes fast (p. 7).
